title: Printing-plate family tree: replicated nanoimprint templates replace array EUV
idea: Like a record plant electroforming many stampers from one master, write a single e-beam master for the honeycomb storage-node and landing-pad layers, replicate it into ~1,000 daughter templates, and print those layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint; each daughter is retired after a fixed wafer count before defects accumulate.
why: Fact 4 (litho capital): retires 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers; imprint tools cost ~1/5-1/10 of EUV with no source power, cutting array patterning cost per layer ~40-60%.

title: Roll-to-roll memory foil laminated onto logic dies
idea: Run 10 um Invar foil through a newspaper-style web line: roll-to-roll sputter the IGZO/high-k/metal stack, pattern every gain-cell level in one pass with a multi-height self-aligned imprint (SAIL) stamp whose step heights encode each mask level, then laser-cut sheets and laminate them onto logic or base-die BEOL.
why: Capital intensity: a web line costs ~1/50 per m2 of a 300 mm fab and the multi-level stamp collapses ~5 masks into one imprint with zero inter-level overlay; density is relaxed (F 50-100 nm), so it targets a cheap capacity tier.

title: Puff-pastry fold-and-bond doubles 3D DRAM tiers each round
idea: Fabricate one complete planar 1T1C tier on thinned donors, then laminate like croissant dough: bond tiers face-to-back in pairs, thin, bond pairs to pairs, so N tiers need only log2(N) sequential bond-thin rounds (5 rounds = 32 tiers) and every tier reuses the proven planar mask set; oversized landing pads absorb ~100 nm bond overlay.
why: Fact 2: reaches the ~26-tier break-even with planar-proven cells, sidestepping the lateral transistor and lateral capacitor; one identical tier flow runs at full volume.

title: Brighton-rock drawn preform sliced into ready-made capacitor wafers
idea: Like seaside rock candy whose lettering is built large and drawn thin, stack a 10 cm glass preform holding thousands of coaxial metal/glass/metal rods, draw and re-stack-draw it (fiber-optic faceplate practice) ~10^5x down to ~40 nm pitch, then saw and polish 10 um slices carrying billions of coaxial capacitors to bond onto transistor wafers.
why: Facts 1 and 4: zero lithography and zero HAR etch for the capacitor; a 10 um-tall coax gives ~6 fF even with glass k~8 because its effective aspect ratio is ~250:1; one preform yields thousands of slices.

title: Deli-slicer nanoskiving: film thickness, not lithography, sets line pitch
idea: Deposit a 2,000-pair laminate of alternating Mo/Ru and oxide, each exactly F thick, on a carrier block, then slice perpendicular to the layers into thin sheets whose cross-sections are atomically uniform line/space gratings ~48 um wide (one mat), and transfer the strips as wordline or bitline arrays.
why: Fact 4: replaces SAQP/EUV line patterning (3-4 litho/spacer loops) with deposition-thickness control at about +/-0.2 nm and near-zero line-edge roughness; one block yields thousands of mat strips, tungsten-free.

title: Permanent-mold casting: reusable mold casts capacitor forests for transfer
idea: Instead of etching a fresh 60:1 mold on every wafer, make one ultra-precise AR>100 mold in single-crystal Si with an anti-stiction release liner, ALD-cast TiN/high-k/TiN shells in it, bond the filled mold to the transistor wafer's landing pads, release the capacitor forest, and reuse the mold ~100x like a die-casting die.
why: Facts 1 and 4: HAR etch and its masks amortize over ~100 wafers, so the mold can use slow, perfect processes; ~2x Cs from taller nodes without per-wafer HAR etch capex.

title: MLCC laminate: interdigitated plates replace the tall pillar capacitor
idea: Copy multilayer-ceramic-capacitor stacking: deposit ~30 alternating TiN and Ru electrode layers separated by 5 nm high-k into a 300 nm stack, cut per-cell blocks, then selectively recess Ru on one sidewall and TiN on the other with different wet chemistries so each wall contacts only odd or only even plates.
why: Fact 1: ~5 fF from a 300 nm stack at AR ~15 (vs 1.5 um at 70:1) on a relaxed non-EUV ~20 nm cell; removes the hardest etch.

title: Jelly-roll winding: strained membranes self-roll into multi-turn capacitors
idea: Borrow Li-ion jelly-roll winding: deposit a planar TiN/high-k/TiN/high-k ribbon on a strained bilayer over a sacrificial film, open one release edge, and let built-in strain roll each ribbon into a 4-6-turn Swiss-roll capacitor lying in a shallow trench.
why: Fact 1: plate area comes from planar ribbon length that cheap litho defines, giving ~4-6x one cylinder's area with no HAR etch.

title: Slip-form pour: grow capacitor pillars upward by dual selective deposition
idea: Like slip-forming a concrete silo that climbs as it pours, grow the storage-node pillar and its mold together from the landing-pad pattern: alternate area-selective ALD of TiN-on-TiN and SiO2-on-SiO2 with inhibitors swapped each supercycle, plus periodic etch-back defect correction, so no deep hole is ever etched.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the 60-75:1 etch (the costliest etch fleet), with no bowing or twisting, allowing AR>100 and ~2x Cs.

title: Glassblowing silicon: hydrogen reflow seals stacked buried cavities for tiers
idea: Use surface-tension shaping like a glassblower: etch deep hole arrays with depth-modulated scallops, then hydrogen-anneal near 1100 C so silicon migrates and pinches each scallop into a sealed planar void (multi-level silicon-on-nothing), leaving stacked single-crystal Si plates that later receive gate and capacitor dielectrics.
why: Fact 2: single-crystal multi-tier silicon without the Si/SiGe superlattice epi that warps and dislocates beyond ~30-60 periods; one etch plus one anneal replaces ~100 epi layers.

title: Crystal casting in hollow molds: lateral selective epitaxy per tier
idea: Build the tier stack from cheap deposited oxide/nitride, carve hollow lateral oxide tubes in each tier off a vertical seed shaft, and grow single-crystal Si laterally inside them from one substrate seed by template-assisted selective epitaxy, casting all tiers' access-transistor channels in one growth run.
why: Fact 2: decouples tier count from epi stack strain, enabling 50-100 tiers on deposition tools ~1/3 the cost of superlattice epi.

title: Float-glass panel interposers made in idle display fabs
idea: Retool underused Gen-6 LCD/OLED backplane lines (each panel ~40 wafers of area) to make 2 um line glass-core interposers and redistribution panels for memory-logic packages, using their existing steppers, sputter and plating, and replacing silicon CoWoS-style interposers for HBM/LPDDR stacks.
why: Fact 6 and capital: unlocks interposer capacity that gates HBM shipments using amortized panel fabs at ~1/5-1/10 the cost per area of 300 mm silicon interposers.

title: Float-line continuous fab: capacitor module never leaves vacuum
idea: Replace the job-shop flow (500+ FOUP moves) with a linear vacuum line like a float-glass or coil-coating line for the capacitor module: mold deposition, HAR etch, clean, ALD electrode, high-k, top electrode and anneal stations chained wafer-by-wafer with in-line metrology at one takt time.
why: Throughput/capital: ~3-4x shorter module cycle time, less WIP capital and queue-time defects, cleanroom only around the line; ~20-30% lower module cost.

title: Tumbling bricks: fluidic self-assembly of DRAM micro-tiles onto logic
idea: Fabricate 200 um trapezoidal DRAM array tiles at one high-yield site, then tumble them in a carrier liquid over logic wafers with matching etched recesses (RFID fluidic assembly style) so shape keys and capillary/solder forces seat each tile, followed by batch bonding and one redistribution layer.
why: Capital/Fact 6: parallel placement of millions of known-good tiles per hour, no TSV stacks or interposers; memory sits on logic like cache.

title: Perfect-binding spine: print stack interconnect on the die edges
idea: Stack thinned DRAM dies like book signatures with all inter-die wiring routed to one polished edge, then pattern vertical interconnect along that spine by laser-direct-write seeding and electroplating, the way a binder glues a spine, eliminating TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV area/yield tax (~3x area per bit, -20-30% yield) and TSV etch/fill/reveal tools; a ~10 um spine pitch still gives thousands of channels per edge.

title: Veneer peeling: controlled spalling yields thin dies and reusable substrates
idea: Like rotary-peeling veneer from a log, deposit a tensile Ni stressor on finished DRAM wafers and peel off a 10-20 um device layer on handle tape for stacking, then reclaim-polish and re-epi the 700 um parent substrate for up to ~5 more uses.
why: Capital and scarce resources: skips backgrind and thinning CMP and cuts quartz-crucible-dependent CZ silicon per bit several-fold.

title: Auto-parts remanufacturing line rebins harvested server DRAM into CXL pools
idea: Run a reman line: robots strip DIMMs from retired servers, packages are desoldered, X-ray screened, burned in and retention-binned, then reballed onto CXL Type-3 expander boards whose controller sets refresh and ECC per bin.
why: Supply without fabs: usable capacity at ~10-20% of new-DRAM cost with zero wafer starts; capital is handlers and testers, not fabs.

title: Contract-brewing program: idle U.S. fabs add BEOL memory layers
idea: As craft brewers rent others' tanks, a federal tolling program buys finished CMOS periphery wafers from foundries and pays idle U.S. 200/300 mm fabs per wafer to add DUV-only, <=350 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory layers, with 5-year guaranteed offtake.
why: U.S. manufacturability/capital: reuses depreciated tools and staff with no EUV and no new shell; output in ~18 months vs 3-5 years for a new fab.

title: Movable-type reticles: tile-stepped array masks shared across products
idea: Like Gutenberg composing pages from reusable type, write a small defect-free array-tile reticle (one mat) and step it repeatedly inside a bladed field, then expose periphery from a type case of standard sense-amp, decoder and I/O tiles; new densities are composed from existing tiles instead of new full reticles.
why: Mask cost/cycle time: small tiles are cheaper and higher-yield to write; derivative mask-set cost falls ~50-70% and tape-out-to-wafer shrinks by weeks.

title: Plywood cross-lamination cancels warp in many-tier stacks
idea: Copy plywood's alternating grain: rotate each tier's line orientation (and its anisotropic film stress) 90 degrees relative to the tier below and alternate tensile/compressive liner recipes, so wafer bow cancels instead of accumulating through the stack.
why: Fact 2/yield: warp and overlay drift cap tier count; cancellation could allow ~2x more tiers before bow exceeds scanner and bonder chuck limits.

title: Nano-Velcro stacking: reworkable HBM dies swapped after test
idea: Replace permanent hybrid bonds with interlocking Cu nanowire hook-and-loop arrays grown in alumina templates that cold-weld under modest pressure yet allow controlled debond; test the stack, pull and replace failing dies, then anneal to make joints permanent.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss instead of scrapping 8-16 good dies for one bad one.

title: Brewed S-layer protein crystals as sub-EUV lithography templates
idea: Ferment bacteria whose surface-layer proteins self-assemble into 2D crystals with hexagonal ~10-15 nm lattices, recrystallize them on wafers over a coarse DUV guide pattern, and use the pores as metal-deposition or etch templates for landing pads and capacitor seeds.
why: Fact 4: lattice period is genetically fixed below EUV pitch and costs grams from a fermenter, replacing an EUV exposure per layer.

title: Volumetric 3D printing: one holographic exposure defines electrode-plus-support lattice
idea: Like volumetric resin printers that cure a whole part at once, expose a 2 um-thick resist with four-beam interference to cure a 3D lattice of vertical posts with horizontal support bridges in one shot, then ALD-replicate it and burn out the resist to leave the capacitor bottom-electrode skeleton with built-in anti-leaning supports.
why: Facts 1 and 4: one exposure replaces mold deposition, support-mesh litho/etch steps and the HAR etch; built-in supports allow AR>100.

title: Spot-color fifth plate: one-mask IGZO gain cell in logic BEOL
idea: Treat a logic flow as a four-color press and add exactly one spot-color plate: one mask patterns an ALD IGZO island between Mn and Mn+1, the existing Mn line serves as bottom gate, and redrawn (not added) via masks form source/drain and read contacts, making a 2T0C gain cell any logic foundry can offer.
why: U.S. manufacturability/capital: DRAM-class embedded memory on existing logic capacity for +1 mask (~3% wafer cost), with no capacitor module and no EUV.

title: Planed wood-grain staircase: one sloped trough exposes every tier
idea: Use the single added mask to open a wide trough at the array edge and etch it through reflowed resist into a 5-10 degree ramp; deposit the tier stack conformally, then CMP flat so each tier surfaces as its own ~400 nm stripe, like grain on a planed board, giving wordline contact landings for all tiers.
why: Capital/throughput: replaces the multi-mask staircase with dozens of trim-etch loops by one mask plus one CMP for 3D DRAM.

title: Embossed relief: one grayscale mask prints three cell levels
idea: Like a relief-embossing die that presses several heights at once, use one grayscale multi-transmission mask on a multi-threshold resist to print landing-pad, bitline-contact and storage-node patterns as three resist heights, then transfer them by sequential etch-back so each level opens self-aligned to the others.
why: Fact 4: adds one mask yet retires two to three critical exposures and their overlay budget; ~5-8% wafer cost reduction.

title: Plate-less holographic print plus one cookie-cutter trim mask
idea: Expose the hexagonal storage-node array by three-beam immersion interference (no mask, perfect periodicity, one spacer pitch split), then use exactly one cheap DUV cookie-cutter mask to blank the pattern outside mats and at mat edges.
why: Fact 4: removes the EUV array-hole layer; interference exposure tools cost roughly a tenth of EUV, with lower roughness and no reticle defects in the array.

title: Kagome basket weave: one grating reticle exposed at three angles
idea: Like triaxial kagome basketry, expose the same line/space grating reticle three times at 0, 60 and 120 degrees (wafer rotated in the pre-aligner between passes) into a hardmask stack that opens only where all three space sets overlap, yielding a hexagonal storage-node hole array from one mask.
why: Fact 4: one cheap, defect-tolerant grating replaces a contact-hole EUV mask; gratings print with the best resolution and depth of focus.

title: Anodized-cookware pores: self-ordered alumina holes beyond 100:1
idea: Deposit 2 um of aluminium over the landing pads, pre-dimple it with the single added mask (10 nm-deep dot pattern), anodize in oxalic acid so pores nucleate at the dimples and grow straight down, open the barrier layer, and ALD the MIM capacitor into the pores.
why: Fact 1: a wet bath produces AR>100 holes at 30-60 nm pitch with no HAR plasma etch, for ~1.5-2x Cs; step capex down ~10x.

title: Rubber-stamp inhibitor printing: the one added master is a stamp
idea: Use a hard-PDMS stamp as the only added pattern master to microcontact-print an ALD inhibitor monolayer in the BEOL, then grow the oxide-semiconductor channel and gate dielectric by area-selective ALD only on unstamped areas, so the memory layer needs no resist, exposure or etch.
why: Capital/steps: replaces ~6 litho/etch/strip steps and scanner time with one stamp contact; a stamp costs ~1% of a mask set.

title: Core-and-cavity casting: radial 3D DRAM from one hole mask
idea: Like sand casting where core prints define internal cavities, deposit a 40-tier stack on the periphery wafer, punch one mask of vertical bitline holes (larger openings on the same mask act as slits), and build each tier's ring IGZO transistor and coaxial capacitor by successive selective lateral recesses and ALD fills from that hole.
why: Facts 2 and 4: array patterning costs one critical mask regardless of tier count, giving a 3D NAND-like cost curve and ~4-8x bits per mask vs 2D.

title: Candle-dipped sidewall channels: ALD thickness sets transistor width
idea: Like dipping candles to build layers on a wick, pattern one mandrel mask, ALD a 3 nm IGZO film on the mandrel sidewalls and etch back so each sidewall becomes a vertical channel whose width is the film thickness; gate dielectric and wordline deposit and recess self-aligned, giving two cells per mandrel.
why: Fact 4: 3 nm device width without EUV; one added mask yields a ~4F2 vertical gain cell above periphery.

title: Origami membrane: one hinge mask folds memory panels into tiers
idea: Fabricate a <=300 nm oxide-semiconductor memory membrane over a sacrificial film and use the one added mask to place SiN/Cr bilayer stress hinges between panels; on release, hinges fold the membrane accordion-style into 4-8 stacked panels over the periphery, with hinge traces as vertical interconnect.
why: Facts 2 and 6: multi-tier memory from one planar flow plus one mask and no TSVs; footprint density x4-8.

title: Zoned newspaper editions: consortium base wafers, one personalization mask
idea: Like papers that print a common edition and swap one plate per zone, a consortium fab runs one standardized DRAM base wafer (array, sense amps, generic I/O) at maximum volume, and each buyer personalizes it with exactly one metal/via mask (density cut, interface, I/O width) on its own BEOL line.
why: Capital: hyperscale volume on one base flow lowers cost per bit, and new entrants need only a ~$0.5-1B BEOL line instead of a $15B fab.

title: Brewery-to-sanitizer conversion: 3D NAND lines build vertical gain cells
idea: Like distilleries switching to hand sanitizer, convert a 3D NAND line during gluts: keep its stack deposition, channel-hole and slit masks and tools, swap the charge-trap fill for an IGZO channel, and add exactly one mask that splits each hole's gate ring into separate write and read gates, forming a 2T0C vertical gain-cell string.
why: Capital/time: DRAM-class bits from existing NAND capacity in months rather than 3-5 years, for +1 mask on an amortized flow.

title: Micro-Czochralski laser seeds: one window mask grows tier crystals
idea: Open seed holes with the one added mask in the inter-tier oxide, deposit amorphous Si above, and melt it with an excimer laser so each hole bottom acts as a tiny Czochralski seed and grain filter, recrystallizing one location-controlled single-crystal grain per array tile for the next tier's access transistors.
why: Fact 2: monolithic stacked tiers with near-single-crystal mobility and a tighter leakage tail, without bonding tools or epi superlattices.

title: Sourdough crumb: porous-silicon capacitors cut by one isolation mask
idea: Like dough fermenting gas pockets, electrochemically porosify a 1 um doped poly-Si layer over the landing pads into ~20 nm random pores, coat with high-k and TiN by ALD, and use the single added coarse mask to cut a cell-isolation grid, so each cell's capacitor is whatever ~15-25 pores fall in it.
why: Fact 1: 10-30x surface-area gain with no hole litho or HAR etch; Cs spread handled by pad sizing and sense-margin binning; bath tool ~1/20 the cost of HAR etch.

title: Thermal-receipt printing: buried metal self-registers the next layer
idea: Like a receipt printer that marks only where heated, flash the wafer with near-IR that buried metal absorbs far more than oxide, so a thermally crosslinking resist hardens only above metal; this registers landing pads to contacts with zero overlay error and no mask, leaving the one allowed new mask for the cut layer.
why: Fact 4: overlay-critical layers without scanner time; overlay error near zero vs the ~2 nm budgets that push layers onto EUV.

title: Score-and-snap glass cutting: notch mask guides crack-defined trenches
idea: Use the single added coarse mask only to place notch crack-starters in a tensile SiN film; a thermal shock then propagates straight, few-nm-wide cracks between notches like scoring and snapping glass, and the cracks are transferred as ultra-narrow cut trenches isolating wordlines or active areas.
why: Fact 4: sub-5 nm cuts over long runs from a DUV mask, replacing an EUV cut layer.

title: Two-angle stencil spraying: one mask, two self-aligned features
idea: Like a painter spraying one stencil from two angles to get two offset strokes, pattern one resist-bridge mask and perform double-angle directional deposition (Dolan-bridge style) so each opening yields two offset, self-aligned features, e.g. access gate plus storage contact, or two cells per opening.
why: Fact 4: halves critical masks for paired features and removes their overlay; ~2x pattern density from one DUV mask.

title: Lego-key bonding: etched studs self-align dies without precision bonders
idea: Use the single added mask to etch tapered studs on the DRAM die and matching sockets on the base wafer; a cheap micron-accurate placer drops dies and gentle vibration seats them so the mechanical keys pull overlay below 100 nm before hybrid bonding.
why: Capital/Fact 6: replaces ~$5M sub-200 nm hybrid bonders with pick-and-place at ~1/5 the cost and several times the throughput.

title: Tie-dye wicking: slit-fed lateral diffusion dopes every tier at once
idea: Like dye wicking into folded cloth, use the single added slit mask to cut through the 3D DRAM tier stack, fill slits with doped glass or vapor dopant, and drive a timed lateral diffusion that forms source/drain junctions in all tiers simultaneously, setting channel length by diffusion distance.
why: Fact 2: lateral-transistor junctions for 50+ tiers in one step, where per-tier implants are impossible; no per-tier masks.

title: Corrugated cardboard flutes: sub-layer recess multiplies tier capacitor area
idea: Deposit each tier's capacitor slab as a fluted superlattice of thin alternating sublayers; after the single added mask opens the capacitor slot, a selective lateral recess etches alternate sublayers to corrugate the slot walls like cardboard flutes, and ALD electrode/high-k/electrode lines the corrugations.
why: Facts 1 and 2: 2-3x capacitor area per lateral 3D cell with no per-tier masks, reaching ~5 fF at shorter lateral length and tighter pitch.

title: Heat-shrink film: relaxed-pitch mask halves pitch on release
idea: Like heat-shrink tubing, print the array at 2x pitch with the single added DUV mask onto a biaxially pre-strained polymer membrane on a carrier, release the strain so features shrink ~50% isotropically, then laminate the shrunken membrane onto the wafer as the etch hardmask.
why: Fact 4: relaxed-pitch printing on a cheap immersion mask replaces EUV or SAQP for one array layer; shrink uniformity across mats is the risk.

title: Turbine-blade EB-PVD columns: seeded columnar growth forms capacitor electrodes
idea: Borrow the electron-beam PVD that grows columnar thermal-barrier coatings on jet blades: place TiN seed dots with the single added mask, then evaporate TiN at grazing incidence with wafer rotation so self-shadowing grows isolated straight 1-2 um columns only on seeds, later coated with high-k and top plate.
why: Facts 1 and 4: high-AR electrodes by deposition with no mold or HAR etch; evaporators cost ~1/5 of HAR etch tools.

title: Multi-head embroidery: write the one added layer maskless per die
idea: Because only one layer is added, write it with a 10,000-beam e-beam direct writer, like a multi-head embroidery machine stitching many garments at once; the mask becomes a data file that changes per product, per lot, or per die to route row and column repair without laser fuses.
why: Mask cost/time: zero reticle spend ($0.5-1M per critical mask), day-scale design turns, and fuse-free per-die repair that lifts yield.
